title: ReCAP Regime-Adaptive Continual Learning for H026 ETF Rotation
description: Implement the ReCAP framework (arXiv:2606.00143, May 2026) as a continual learning layer for the H026 ETF rotation strategy, addressing the regime-shift degradation problem. ReCAP integrates continual learning into portfolio management via: (1) Adaptive Regime Detection Module — segments historical ETF return data into variable-length regimes using change-point detection (not fixed IS/OOS splits); (2) Policy Library — learns a regime-specific allocation policy vector for each detected regime and stores it; (3) Rapid Adaptation — when a new regime is detected, retrieves the most similar historical regime policy and fine-tunes online, avoiding catastrophic forgetting. H384 tests ReCAP as a meta-layer on top of H026 ETF rotation: instead of fixed 12m momentum ranking, train a lightweight DRL policy per detected regime that learns which ETF selection heuristics (momentum window, OB filter, SPY 200MA overlay) work best in each regime. Gate: OOS Sharpe > 2.610 (H346 canonical OB-filtered baseline). IS: 2008-2020 (used for policy library), OOS: 2021-2026. Script: backtesting/daily/run_h384_recap_continual.py (to be written). Requires: PyTorch, ruptures (change-point detection), stable-baselines3.
rationale: H026 is our core 27% production allocation and has 18+ years of confirmed OOS data. The main risk to H026 is regime shifts — the 2022 rate shock, COVID (2020), GFC (2008) each represent distinct market regimes where different ETFs dominate. ReCAP's policy library approach is superior to H346's static OB filter because: (1) it adapts online as regimes evolve; (2) it avoids the IS/OOS split problem by treating every regime shift as a new task; (3) it preserves knowledge from prior regimes (catastrophic forgetting mitigation). The regime segmentation aligns with our macro regime framework (FRED data: SPY 200MA, VIX, yield curve). This is also directly relevant to the dream cycle's research challenge: our hypothesis tests use fixed IS/OOS splits that may not generalize to future regimes — ReCAP's approach suggests designing strategies that adapt to detected regime shifts rather than assuming stationarity.
